# Lao sticky rice (khao niao)

Sticky rice soaked, steamed and kept warm in a covered basket, then pinched off and rolled into small balls by children's own hands. In Laos and in Lao homes everywhere, sticky rice is shared from one basket and eaten with the fingers.

## Makes enough for

6 children

## Ingredients

- 2 cups sticky rice (also sold as glutinous or sweet rice)
- cool water for rinsing and soaking
- 1 small cucumber, if we like

## Tools

- a large bowl for soaking
- a strainer
- a bamboo sticky rice basket (huad) and its pot, or a steamer basket lined with a damp cloth
- an induction hot plate
- a lid or a damp cloth to cover the rice
- a large tray or shallow bowl
- a rice paddle or flat wooden spoon
- a covered rice basket (tip khao) or a bowl with a damp cloth
- a small bowl of water for wetting hands
- one child knife and cutting board for each child who is cutting
- measuring cups
- a plate for each child

## Steps

- Wash our hands with soap and water.
- Measure the rice into the large bowl and rinse it in cool water, swishing with our hands, until the water runs almost clear.
- Cover the rice with plenty of cool water and let it soak for at least 4 hours, or overnight.
- Pour the rice into the strainer and let it drain.
- An adult puts a few inches of water in the pot and brings it to a boil.
- Spoon the rice into the steamer basket.
- An adult sets the basket over the boiling water and covers the rice.
- Steam the rice for about 15 minutes, until the grains on top look shiny.
- An adult flips the rice over in one piece and steams it about 10 minutes more, until every grain is soft and see-through.
- An adult turns the rice out onto the tray and spreads it with the paddle to let the steam out.
- Gather the rice into the covered basket to keep it warm and soft.
- Wash the cucumber under running water.
- Cut the cucumber into sticks with child knives.
- Wash our hands well again, since everyone touches the food.
- Dip our fingers in the bowl of water.
- Pinch off a small piece of rice and roll it in our palm into a little ball.
- Eat it with our fingers, with a cucumber stick alongside.

## Why we use it

Rolling a small ball of warm sticky rice in one palm builds hand strength (fine motor development). Children watch the rice change through soaking and steaming. Eating from a shared basket with our hands lets children eat sticky rice the way it is eaten in Lao homes. Sticky rice has no gluten, even though it is sometimes called glutinous rice.

## I wonder

- I wonder why this rice sticks together when other rice falls apart.
- I wonder what happens to the rice grains while they soak.
- I wonder how steam can cook food.

## Connections

- Children can compare a few dry grains with soaked grains and steamed grains.
- The cloudy rinse and soaking water goes on a garden bed.
- Cucumbers come from our summer beds and the weekly produce bin.

## Cutting for our youngest

- Cucumber is a soft first food for child knives. Children cut sticks with an adult close beside each child who is cutting (close supervision). The others can rinse rice or fill the water bowl.
- Children wait until the rice is cool enough to touch before they roll it.
- Children eat sitting down with an adult nearby.

## Clean up

- Rinse water goes on a garden bed.
- Children scrape the stuck rice off their hands into the compost and wash their hands.
- Cucumber ends go to the compost.
- Child knives. Washed one at a time, never left in a sink of water, dried and returned to the knife roll with the blades covered.
- Cutting boards. Scrubbed with hot soapy water, rinsed, sanitized and stood upright to dry.
- Bowl, strainer and measuring cups. Children may wash and dry them. The educator rewashes as needed.
- Steamer basket. Rinsed with cool water, scrubbed of stuck grains and left to air dry fully.
- Pot, tray and rice paddle. Washed and dried by the educator.
- Induction hot plate. Cooled, surface wiped.
- Children sweep their own space with the dustpan and brush. The educator finishes and checks each tool before it is put away.

# Lao sticky rice (khao niao)

Sticky rice (khao niao) is the everyday rice of Laos. It is soaked, steamed and kept warm in a covered woven basket (tip khao), then pinched off and rolled into small balls by hand. In Lao homes it is shared from one basket and eaten with the fingers, dipped in jeow or eaten with khai paen.

## Makes enough for

6 children

## Ingredients

- 2 cups sticky rice (also sold as glutinous or sweet rice)
- water for rinsing and soaking
- 1 small cucumber, if we like
- 3 ripe tomatoes, for the jeow, if we like
- 2 cloves garlic in their skins, for the jeow, if we like
- 1 small shallot in its skin, for the jeow, if we like
- 1 green onion, for the jeow, if we like
- a small handful of cilantro, for the jeow, if we like
- a pinch of salt, for the jeow, if we like
- 1 chili, kept on the side, if we like
- 2 khai paen sheets (Lao river weed), if we like
- 1 teaspoon oil, for the khai paen, if we like

## Tools

- a large bowl for soaking
- a colander
- a bamboo steamer basket (huad), or a steamer basket lined with a damp cloth
- a soup pot for steaming
- an induction hot plate
- a damp cloth to cover the rice
- a large tray or shallow bowl
- a rice paddle or flat wooden spoon
- a sticky rice basket with a lid (tip khao), or a bowl with a damp cloth
- a small bowl, with water for wetting hands
- a pan
- a mortar and pestle
- culinary scissors
- a child knife for each child
- a cutting board for each child
- measuring cups
- a plate for each child

## Steps

- Wash our hands with soap and water.
- Measure the rice into the large bowl and rinse it in cool water, swishing with our hands, until the water runs almost clear.
- Cover the rice with plenty of cool water and let it soak for at least 4 hours, or overnight.
- Pour the rice into the colander and let it drain.
- An adult puts a few inches of water in the pot and brings it to a boil.
- Spoon the rice into the steamer basket.
- An adult sets the basket over the boiling water and covers the rice.
- Steam the rice for about 15 minutes, until the grains on top look shiny.
- An adult flips the rice over in one piece and steams it about 10 minutes more, until every grain is soft and see-through.
- An adult turns the rice out onto the tray and spreads it with the paddle to let the steam out.
- Gather the rice into the covered basket to keep it warm and soft.
- An adult roasts the tomatoes, garlic and shallot in the pan, with no oil, until the skins blister and blacken in spots.
- Let them cool until they are safe to touch.
- Peel the garlic and shallot with our fingers.
- Pound the garlic and shallot in the mortar.
- Add the tomatoes and pound them into a chunky dip.
- Tear the cilantro and green onion over the top, and add a pinch of salt.
- An adult crisps the khai paen in a little oil in the pan for a few seconds on each side.
- Snip the khai paen into small squares with culinary scissors.
- Wash the cucumber under running water.
- Cut the cucumber into sticks with child knives.
- Wash our hands well again, since everyone touches the food.
- Dip our fingers in the bowl of water.
- Pinch off a small piece of rice and roll it in our palm into a little ball.
- Dip a ball of rice in the jeow, or eat it with a square of khai paen or a cucumber stick.

## Where it comes from

- Sticky rice is the rice eaten every day in Laos, and in Lao homes here.
- Jeow is the Lao word for a dipping sauce. Jeow mak len is made from roasted tomatoes. It is usually made with fish sauce and chili, and since our kitchen is vegetarian we use salt and keep the chili on the side.
- Khai paen comes from Luang Prabang in northern Laos. River weed is gathered from the Mekong and the rivers that run into it during the dry months. It is pressed into sheets with garlic, tomato and sesame and dried in the sun.
- If we cannot find khai paen, roasted seaweed (nori) can sit beside the rice. Nori is eaten in Japan and Korea, so we name it as theirs.

## Why we use it

Rolling a small ball of warm sticky rice in one palm builds hand strength (fine motor development). Pounding jeow in a mortar builds strength in the hands and arms (heavy work and strong force, proprioceptive input). Children watch the rice change through soaking and steaming. Eating from a shared basket with our hands lets children eat sticky rice the way it is eaten in Lao homes. Sticky rice has no gluten, even though it is sometimes called glutinous rice. Khai paen has sesame on it, so we check each child's allergies first.

## I wonder

- I wonder why this rice sticks together when other rice falls apart.
- I wonder what happens to the rice grains while they soak.
- I wonder how steam can cook food.
- I wonder how a plant from a river can become a flat sheet.

## Connections

- Children can compare a few dry grains with soaked grains and steamed grains.
- The cloudy rinse and soaking water goes on a garden bed.
- Cucumbers, tomatoes, cilantro and green onions come from our summer beds and the weekly produce bin.

## Cutting for our youngest

- Cucumber is a soft first food for child knives. Children cut sticks with an adult close beside each child who is cutting (close supervision). The others can rinse rice, peel garlic or fill the water bowl.
- Khai paen and seaweed are snipped into small pieces for children under four (choking hazard).
- Children wait until the rice and roasted tomatoes are cool enough to touch.
- Children eat sitting down with an adult nearby.

## Clean up

- Rinse water goes on a garden bed.
- Children scrape the stuck rice off their hands into the compost and wash their hands.
- Cucumber ends, tomato cores and garlic and shallot skins go to the compost.
- Child knives. Washed one at a time, never left in a sink of water, dried and returned to the knife roll with the blades covered.
- Cutting boards. Scrubbed with hot soapy water, rinsed, sanitized and stood upright to dry.
- Bowl, colander and measuring cups. Children may wash and dry them. The educator rewashes as needed.
- Mortar and pestle. Children may scrub them with warm water. The educator rewashes as needed.
- Culinary scissors. Opened fully to wash the hinge, dried and stored closed.
- Steamer basket. Rinsed with cool water, scrubbed of stuck grains and left to air dry fully.
- Pot, pan, tray and rice paddle. Washed and dried by the educator.
- Induction hot plate. Cooled, surface wiped.
- Children sweep their own space with the dustpan and brush. The educator finishes and checks each tool before it is put away.
